summary: Requires that the IETF never publish any IETF Stream RFC without IETF rough consensus. It updates RFC 2026, the document describing the standards process.

plainLanguage.summary: A club rule: nothing is published under the club's name unless most members broadly agree.

questions: do ietf stream rfcs need consensus
what does rfc 8789 change in rfc 2026
do ietf stream rfcs need rough consensus
where do documents without ietf consensus get published
subtitle: A one-rule process change: the IETF must not publish IETF Stream RFCs without rough consensus.

tldr.problem: RFC 2026 let the IESG approve Informational or Experimental RFCs for publication without IETF rough consensus.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8789 says the IETF MUST NOT publish RFCs on the IETF Stream without establishing IETF rough consensus for publication.
tldr.outcome: Documents the community cannot agree on have other routes, the Independent Stream or, for research, the IRTF Stream.

today: RFC 8789 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 9) that updates RFC 2026, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Gap in RFC 2026
sections.content:
The procedures in RFC 2026 allow Informational or Experimental RFCs to be published without IETF rough consensus. That RFC predates the separation of the various streams (IRTF, IAB and Independent); when it was written, there were only RFCs.

As a consequence, the IESG was permitted to approve an Internet-Draft for publication as an RFC without IETF rough consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook was written before there were separate shelves for different kinds of papers, and it left a loophole.

sections.title: The Rule
sections.content: The action is a single sentence: the IETF MUST NOT publish RFCs on the IETF Stream without establishing IETF rough consensus for publication. The document is BCP 9 and updates RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything goes out under the IETF's name, most people involved must broadly agree. No exceptions.

sections.title: Why the 2007 Statement Was Not Enough
sections.content:
In 2007 the IESG issued a statement that no document would be issued without first conducting an IETF Last Call. The RFC argues this apparently improved matters but made them worse: rather than publishing documents without verifying rough consensus, the IESG was explicitly publishing documents that had failed to achieve it.

The RFC acknowledges that some documents the community cannot agree on may still need publishing. It points to the Independent Stream for those, or the IRTF Stream for research documents, which explicitly publishes minority opinion Informational RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: An earlier fix made people hold a last call first, but then papers that lost the vote still got printed. Papers nobody agrees on can go on a different shelf.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The document has no IANA actions and introduces no new security considerations. The RFC adds that the procedure will prevent publication of IETF Stream documents that have not reached rough consensus about their security aspects, thus potentially improving their security.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only a rule about paperwork, but agreeing before printing may also catch safety problems.
